'''''Saccharum officinarum''''' is a large, strong-growing species of [[Poaceae|grass]] in the [[sugarcane]] genus. Its stout stalks are rich in [[sucrose]], a [[disaccharide]] [[sugar]] which accumulates in the [[Plant stem|stalk internodes]]. It originated in [[New Guinea]],<ref>In [[New Guinea]], according to sources cited by Christian Daniels in Joseph Needham, ''Science and Civilisation in China'', Volume 6.3,  p. 129ff; Warner, John N. “Sugar Cane: An Indigenous Papuan Cultigen.” ''Ethnology'', vol. 1, no. 4, 1962, pp. 405–11.</ref> and is now cultivated in tropical and subtropical countries worldwide for the [[Sugar industry|production]] of [[sugar]], [[ethanol]] and other products. It is one of the most productive and most intensively cultivated kinds of sugarcane.

==Description==
''Saccharum officinarum'', a [[perennial]] plant, grows in clumps consisting of a number of strong unbranched stems. A network of [[rhizome]]s forms under the soil which sends up secondary shoots near the parent plant. The stems vary in colour, being green, pinkish, or purple and can reach {{convert|5|m|abbr=off}} in height. They are jointed, nodes being present at the bases of the alternate [[leaves]]. The internodes contain a fibrous white pith immersed in sugary sap. The elongated, linear, green leaves have thick midribs and saw-toothed edges and grow to a length of about {{convert|30|to|60|cm|abbr=off}} and width of {{convert|5|cm|abbr=on|sigfig=1}}.

The terminal inflorescence is a [[panicle]] up to {{convert|60|cm|abbr=on}} long, a pinkish plume that is broadest at the base and tapering towards the top. The [[spikelet]]s are borne on side branches and are about {{convert|3|mm|frac=16}} long and are concealed in tufts of long, silky hair. The fruits are dry and each one contains a single seed.<ref name=Kew>{{cite web |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:419977-1 |title=''Saccharum officinarum''|publisher=Kew Royal Botanic Gardens|location=Kew|access-date=2012-09-21}}</ref><ref name=FAO>{{cite web |url=http://www.fao.org/ag/AGP/AGPC/doc/GBASE/data/Pf000310.HTM |title=''Saccharum officinarum'' L. |publisher=[[FAO]] |access-date=2012-09-21 |archive-date=2014-01-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140109084313/http://www.fao.org/ag/AGP/AGPC/doc/GBASE/data/Pf000310.HTM |url-status=dead }}</ref> Sugarcane harvest typically occurs before the plants flower, as the flowering process causes a reduction in sugar content.<ref>"[http://www.ogtr.gov.au/internet/ogtr/publishing.nsf/content/sugarcane-3/$FILE/biologysugarcane.pdf The Biology and Ecology of Sugarcane (''Saccharum'' spp. hybrids) in Australia], Australian Government, Department of Health and Ageing, Office of the Gene Technology Regulator, 2004; p. 10.</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
{{Further|Sugarcane#History}}

''Saccharum officinarum'' was first domesticated in [[New Guinea]] and the islands east of the [[Wallace Line]] by [[Indigenous people of New Guinea|Papuans]], where it is the modern center of diversity. Beginning at around 6,000 [[Before Present|BP]] it was [[selectively bred]] from the native ''[[Saccharum robustum|S. robustum]]''. From New Guinea it spread westwards to [[Island Southeast Asia]] after contact with [[Austronesians]], where it [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridized]] with ''[[Saccharum spontaneum|S. spontaneum]]''.<ref name="Paterson2012">{{cite book |last1=Paterson |first1=Andrew H. |title=Genomics of the Saccharinae |last2=Moore |first2=Paul H. |last3=Tom L. |first3=Tew |publisher=[[Springer Science & Business Media]]|year=2012 |isbn=9781441959478 |editor1-last=Paterson |editor1-first=Andrew H. |pages=43–72 |chapter=The Gene Pool of ''Saccharum'' Species and Their Improvement |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=F282fp_IMI8C&pg=PA54}}</ref>

It can interbreed with other sugarcane species, such as ''[[Saccharum sinense|S. sinense]]'' and ''[[Saccharum barberi|S. barberi]]''. 
The major commercial [[cultivar]]s are complex [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]].<ref>{{cite journal|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|last1=Vilela|first1=Mariane de Mendonça|last2=Del Bem|first2=Luiz Eduardo|last3=Van Sluys|first3=Marie-Anne|last4=de Setta|first4=Nathalia|last5=Kitajima|first5=João Paulo|last6=Cruz|first6=Guilherme Marcelo Queiroga|last7=Sforça|first7=Danilo Augusto|last8=de Souza|first8=Anete Pereira|last9=Ferreira|first9=Paulo Cavalcanti Gomes|last10=Grativol|first10=Clícia|last11=Cardoso-Silva|first11=Claudio Benicio|title=Analysis of Three Sugarcane Homo/Homeologous Regions Suggests Independent Polyploidization Events of ''Saccharum officinarum'' and ''Saccharum spontaneum''|journal=[[Genome Biology and Evolution]] |date=2017 |volume=9|issue=2|pages=266–278|doi=10.1093/gbe/evw293|pmid=28082603|pmc=5381655}}</ref>

== Pests ==
''S. officinarum'' is a common host of the oriental beetle (''[[Exomala orientalis]]''). During their larval stage, these beetles feed on the roots of the plant which affects its growth. Current pesticides are still being researched.<ref>{{Cite report |title=Exomala orientalis (oriental beetle) |last=CABI |date=2022-01-07 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.5510 |language=en|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Uses ==

Portions of the stem of this and several other species of sugarcane have been used from ancient times for chewing to extract the sweet juice. It was cultivated in New Guinea about 8,000 years ago for this purpose. Extraction of the juice and boiling to concentrate it was probably first done in India more than 2,000 years ago.<ref name="Kew" />

''Saccharum officinarum'' and its hybrids are grown for the production of sugar, ethanol, and other industrial uses in tropical and subtropical regions around the world. The stems and the [[byproduct]]s of the sugar industry are used for feeding to [[livestock]]. [[Pig]]s fed on sugarcane juice and a [[Soybean|soy]]-based [[protein supplement]] produced stronger piglets that grow faster than those on a more conventional diet.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/003/w3647e/W3647E03.htm#ch3 |title=Sugar cane |work=Feeding pigs in the tropics |publisher=[[FAO]]|access-date=2012-09-21}}</ref> As its specific name (''officinarum'', "of dispensaries") implies, it is also used in traditional medicine both internally and externally.<ref name=Kew/>

About 70% of the sugar produced worldwide comes from ''S. officinarum'' and hybrids using this species.<ref name=kew2>{{cite web| title=Plants & Fungi: Saccharum officinarum (sugar cane)| publisher=[[Royal Botanical Gardens, Kew]]| url=http://www.kew.org/plants-fungi/Saccharum-officinarum.htm| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120604003442/http://www.kew.org/plants-fungi/Saccharum-officinarum.htm| archive-date=2012-06-04}}</ref>
